analysis.one_liner: Removes the $75 million cap on what oil companies must pay for offshore oil spills.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made offshore oil companies pay the full cost of spills instead of capping their liability at $75 million, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when an offshore oil rig spills oil into American waters, the company responsible must pay all cleanup costs plus damages, but only up to $75 million beyond cleanup. Taxpayers cover the rest. This bill would have erased that cap, making the polluting company pay everything: lost livelihoods, damaged fisheries and coastlines, property losses, and the cost of extra public services like fire protection during a spill response. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, tourism businesses, and taxpayers. When a spill exceeds the cap, the public currently foots the bill for damages and restoration; this bill would have shifted that cost onto the companies that cause the spills. It also would have given fishing, tourism, and property owners a fuller route to compensation for revenue and profit losses.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million cap on damages, making the responsible party liable for the full amount of all covered damages, including lost natural resources, property, revenue, and profits.
Requires polluters to cover the costs of increased public services during or after spill cleanup, such as fire protection, which today can fall on local governments and taxpayers.
The bill's stated purpose is to require oil polluters to pay the full cost of oil spills rather than capping their liability.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil companies, which would lose the protection of the $75 million liability cap and become responsible for the entire cost of spills they cause, including damages that can run into the billions after major disasters like the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill.

drawbacks.text: Uncapped liability could make insurance harder or more expensive to obtain for offshore drilling, and critics of unlimited liability argue that some cost of rare catastrophic spills would show up in energy prices and in the willingness of firms to insure offshore projects.

Supporters might face the objection that unlimited, retroactive-style liability provisions can be difficult to underwrite and could push smaller operators out, concentrating offshore drilling in the largest companies. The bill text and summary provided do not address insurance availability or transition issues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple: shift the cost of oil spill disasters from taxpayers and coastal communities to the companies that profit from drilling. The main honest objection is that uncapped liability could raise the cost or difficulty of insuring offshore operations, but a spill like Deepwater Horizon caused tens of billions in damages against a $75 million cap, so the public exposure under current law is far larger than the industry-cost concern.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced near the end of the session and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 21, 2020, sponsored by Senator Menendez with nine Democratic cosponsors including Booker, Blumenthal, Reed, Markey, Klobuchar, Feinstein, Merkley, Durbin, and Gillibrand.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action was recorded; the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies came out ahead: the $75 million cap on their spill liability survived, leaving taxpayers and coastal communities to cover damages beyond that limit. No committee hearing or vote was ever scheduled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies kept their liability cap

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored; the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the $75 million cap on their liability for offshore spills, exposing them to the full cost of disasters like Deepwater Horizon, which cost tens of billions. Keeping the cap means the public picks up spill costs above $75 million, so the industry's interest in the status quo runs directly against taxpayers' and coastal communities'.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses suffer revenue and profit losses when spills hit their waters, and the bill explicitly made revenue and profit losses recoverable in full rather than capped. Their interest runs alongside coastal residents' and taxpayers'.
Unlimited liability would have increased the exposure insurers underwrite for offshore drilling, likely raising premiums, while also potentially increasing demand for spill insurance.
